summary: Shoppers pick a USB-C charger by the device it must feed: the watts that device accepts first, then what the laptop port keeps once a phone is plugged in, then price and extras such as a retractable cable or a display. Since September 2026 the phone tier has moved from 30-45 W to 60 W with a protocol condition: Apple says iPhone 18 Pro needs a 60 W-capable charger with AVS and USB-PD 3.2, and the Galaxy S26 Ultra needs PPS at 20 V/3 A, so wattage alone no longer settles the phone question. In the last 60 days UGREEN added AVS to its $39.99 Nexode Air 65W, Baseus launched the 100 W PicoGo Pro AH22, Twelve South launched a 65 W retractable charger with UK/EU plugs, and Black Friday put the Anker Prime 100W at $39.99 on Amazon.

axes.why: ChatGPT split its picks by watts in 5 of 6 chats (30, 45, 65/67, 100, 100+). Android Authority's guide ranks on output per port, and Apple publishes a fast-charge wattage for each iPhone and MacBook.

breakpoints.why: Apple: iPhone 17e and iPhone Air fast charge (50% in around 30 minutes) with 20 W or higher.
Apple: iPhone 17, 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max reach 50% in around 20 minutes with 40 W or higher.

Apple: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max reach 50% in around 15 minutes only with a 60 W-capable adapter that uses AVS and supports USB-PD 3.2. Android Authority: Galaxy S26 Ultra's 60 W needs PPS with 20 V/3 A from one port.
The tier ChatGPT gives for a phone, tablet and thin laptop; searched as 'best 65w usb c charger for laptop'.
Apple: MacBook Air (2022 or later) fast charges with 70 W, 96 W or 140 W adapters; 67 W counts only for the 13.6-inch models.
USB-IF: before PD 3.1, USB PD stopped at 100 W (20 V over a 5 A cable). Apple: the 14-inch MacBook Pro fast charges at 96 W or 140 W, so the 100 W class is the first that qualifies.
Apple: the 16-inch MacBook Pro fast charges only with 140 W. USB-IF: the 28 V fixed voltage enables 140 W.
USB-IF: the 48 V fixed voltage enables 240 W, the top of USB PD.

axes.label: Whether the charger speaks the mode the phone needs for top speed (AVS, PPS)
axes.why: ChatGPT raised PPS or a proprietary protocol in 3 of 6 chats ('wattage alone won't establish compatibility'). Apple now names AVS as a condition, and Android Authority says the S26 Ultra's 20 V PPS mode is less common than PPS itself.

breakpoints.why: Apple: a third-party adapter must be 60 W-capable, use AVS and support USB-PD 3.2 for iPhone 18 Pro's 15-minute tier. 9to5Mac: a 96 W or 140 W MacBook charger lacks AVS.
Android Authority (Robert Triggs): the S26 Ultra needs a USB PD 3.1 charger with PPS and 20 V/3 A from a single port; it measured 42 minutes to full on Samsung's 60 W adapter.
USB-IF: the 28 V fixed voltage is what delivers 140 W; a PD 3.0 charger tops out at 100 W.

axes.label: Watts the laptop port keeps when a second device is plugged in
axes.why: Android Authority lists power splitting as a ranking criterion and prints each pick's split. ChatGPT separated its picks by split (45+20, 65+30, 65+35).

breakpoints.why: 65-67 W chargers fall to about 45 W on the laptop port with a second device. Android Authority gives 45/12/10 W for the Anker Prime 67W with three devices.
100 W chargers keep a 65 W laptop at full speed with a phone attached. Android Authority gives 65/35 W for the Anker Prime 100W.
Two 100 W laptops at once needs 200 W total and two ports at the pre-PD 3.1 ceiling of 100 W each.

axes.why: ChatGPT sorted its picks into one USB-C (phone only), two USB-C plus USB-A (everyday 65-67 W) and at least two USB-C (laptop and phone). Android Authority lists port count and type as a criterion.

rules: A charger's headline watts is its total; the figure that decides a purchase is what one port gives one device, and what that port keeps once a second device is plugged in. Researchers should take the split from the maker's output table or a named test (Android Authority prints splits), never from the headline. For phones, the phone maker's statement counts: Apple's support page for iPhone (60 W-capable, AVS, USB-PD 3.2 for iPhone 18 Pro) and Android Authority's S26 Ultra test (PPS at 20 V/3 A). A 100 W or 140 W charger without AVS does not give an iPhone 18 Pro its top tier, and a '65 W PPS' charger may stop at 45 W on a Samsung. For laptops, Apple's MacBook page sets 70, 96 and 140 W; 140 W needs PD 3.1 at 28 V. Traps: 'dynamic 45-60 W' is a maker's phrase and is not proof of AVS; AVS claims need the maker's spec sheet or a ChargerLAB test; Amazon titles omit model numbers, so the ASIN must be matched to the model; Black Friday prices read on 2026-11-27 will lapse.
